title: Quality of the supervision, training and of the two-way transfer of knowledge between the researcher and the host
content:
## 1.3 Quality of the supervision, training and of the two-way transfer of knowledge between the researcher and the host

### 1.3.1 Qualifications and experience of the supervisory team

FIELDWISE is a European Fellowship hosted by Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, over a confirmed 30-month duration comprising a 24-month fellowship at ELTE (M1–M24) and a 6-month non-academic placement (M25–M30). Supervision is deliberately configured as a two-person team at the beneficiary, matched to the dual character of the objective set — physiological grounding of the stress target and scalable geospatial prediction — so that no methodological demand of the project falls outside a named supervisor's competence. This is a direct answer to the sub-criterion's demand for supervisory qualifications and experience appropriate to the science.

The lead supervisor is Prof. András Jung, Professor at the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, whose expertise spans remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging and field spectroscopy, and geoinformatics. This is the precise match for the project's methodological core: the proximal-hyperspectral-to-Sentinel bridge (O2) and the host's own hyperspectral instrumentation — the Ultris S5 (VIS-NIR narrow bands) and the Cubert CUVIS Lab Lite — sit squarely within his field. He chairs the Project Steering Group and is the escalation point for scientific method and for the training plan. Critically for the assessment of supervisory experience, the supervisor and the host institute have already operated at exactly this level together: they previously prepared and submitted an MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowship application, PLANTDIGISENSE, with the same fellow and the same host institute — evidence of a functioning, tested supervisory relationship rather than a first encounter. FIELDWISE is thus a resubmission whose supervision has been rehearsed once already.

The co-supervisor is Dr. Roland Hollós, of the ELTE Department of Meteorology, whose expertise is machine learning and meta-modelling of crop and grassland multi-model outputs, and agro-meteorology. He carries a defined and non-overlapping responsibility: the methodological lead and quality assurance for model development and testing across the *Prospective and Uncertainty-Aware Prediction* and *Temporal and Cross-Country Transferability* work packages. This places the project's principal statistical-modelling risk — the Bayesian/hierarchical modelling, uncertainty quantification and transfer-learning/domain-adaptation components on which O3 and O4 depend — under dedicated methodological oversight, while the fellow designs, builds and runs the work. The result is a supervision configuration that is interdisciplinary within the beneficiary itself (cartography/geoinformatics alongside meteorology/machine learning), the intra-host counterpart of the project's interdisciplinary science.

Supervision is further complemented by a named scientific advisor at Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem (Hungarian University of Agriculture and Life Sciences), Prof. Gábor Milics — Hungary's country representative to the International Society of Precision Agriculture, working on remote sensing in precision agriculture — who advises the fellow personally and adds a second, agronomy-facing supervision strand outside the formal governance structure. The fellow is therefore mentored across the two disciplines the project spans.

### 1.3.2 Planned training activities: scientific, management and transferable skills

Training is organised through a Career Development Plan, delivered as the early deliverable D1.3 Career Development Plan, established jointly by both supervisors and the fellow, agreed by M3 and reviewed at five points across the action (M6, M12, M16, M20 and M27, the last falling inside the placement where non-academic career development is most in play). The plan is the instrument through which the four training strands below are agreed, tracked and revised.

**Scientific and technical training.** The fellowship closes a specific, named competence gap — Bayesian modelling, spatio-temporal AI, sensor transfer, uncertainty, domain adaptation and decision evaluation — by delivering the eleven host-to-fellow competences (§1.3.3) as supervised practice on the project's own work packages, plus named ELTE short courses. Because the training content is the research programme itself, each competence is exercised against a real deliverable rather than in the abstract: for example, uncertainty quantification is trained while producing the calibrated forecasts of O3, and domain adaptation while producing the Hungary→Bulgaria adaptation protocol of O4. The intended outcome is advanced competence in Bayesian/probabilistic modelling, uncertainty quantification, spatio-temporal validation, sensor-domain transfer, cross-country adaptation, operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation and IP/exploitation.

**Management and research-leadership training.** Project management, grant writing, and IP and exploitation form a distinct strand, the last delivered against a concrete live question — the ownership of work done on the fellow's DrR - Digital Agronomist background IP inside a commercial partner during the placement — so that IP training is anchored in a real decision rather than a generic module.

**Transferable skills.** Seven strands are planned: research integrity; open science and FAIR practice; generative-AI literacy; grant writing; IP and exploitation; project management; and science communication. This directly satisfies the call's mandatory scope requirement (SR-04) that training integrate key transferable and digital skills — including generative AI — and foster an Open Science culture, knowledge valorisation and good scientific conduct including research integrity, and it maps onto the expected outcome of an increased set of research and transferable skills leading to improved employability within academia and beyond (EO-01).

**Teaching and public engagement.** Research results feed back into host teaching (EO-08) through three measures: co-designing and delivering a full module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture; supervising one ELTE MSc thesis; and co-supervising the field-experiment component of one PhD student's work. Teaching is framed honestly as an existing strength transferred rather than a competence to acquire — the fellow taught for five years at Agricultural University Plovdiv, including syllabus design, lecturing and examining in Bulgarian and English and Bachelor's thesis supervision — with the developmental content being the move to a new discipline, a new institution and a new language of instruction, and the step up from Bachelor's to Master's and doctoral supervision. Networking and communication (EO-03) are pursued through publications built around four principal scientific outputs (P1–P4), at least two peer-reviewed submissions during or shortly after the fellowship, one public field demonstration with AgroVIR farmers, and one public-facing article each year. The supervision cadence supporting all of this is concrete: a weekly one-to-one with the supervisor; a weekly technical session with the co-supervisor through the prediction and transferability work packages (M6–M21), tapering to monthly outside that window; a monthly written progress record held by the fellow; and a quarterly review against the Career Development Plan attended by both supervisors. Together these arrangements evidence the quality and sustainability of research training and supervision the call seeks (EO-05).

### 1.3.3 Two-way transfer of knowledge between the researcher and the host

As a European Fellowship, the knowledge transfer required and delivered is genuinely two-way between the researcher and the host — there is no outgoing-phase third party — and FIELDWISE is designed so that neither direction is nominal. **Host → fellow:** ELTE transfers geoinformatics; EO time-series analysis; optical/SAR integration; hyperspectral-to-multispectral transfer; spatio-temporal modelling; Bayesian hierarchical modelling; uncertainty quantification; transfer learning/domain adaptation; reproducible geospatial computation; research software/web deployment; and IP and research exploitation. **Fellow → host:** the researcher transfers plant physiology; horticultural crop science; plant protection/agronomy; water-stress experimentation; physiological phenotyping; hyperspectral field measurements; biological interpretation of Earth observation; the DrR - Digital Agronomist preliminary development; and access to complementary agricultural research collaborations. The transfer is therefore bidirectional in substance (crop physiology/agronomy ↔ geospatial/data science), not a one-directional upskilling: the fellow brings a physiological and agronomic domain the host's remote-sensing group does not itself hold, and the host gains a durable biological-interpretation and field-experimentation capability alongside a working crop-science prototype. Because this exchange is institutionalised through the co-supervision structure and the weekly integration cadence, it strengthens the host's R&I capacity and improves its transfer of knowledge (EO-07) and forges, for the fellow, the new mind-sets and approaches the call expects from international, inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary experience (EO-02).

The two-way transfer at the host is embedded in a wider academic–research–industry knowledge chain that gives the fellowship its inter-sectoral and international reach: Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem contributes the long-term experimental knowledge and the source-domain dataset for model development and validation; Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute contributes the independent Bulgarian research environment for a genuine Hungary→Bulgaria cross-country transferability test rather than a mere increase in sample size; and AGROVIR Kft. bridges research field to farmer field and research prototype to operational requirement. Each partner is the environment in which one of the project's transferability rungs is actually reached, so the knowledge chain is structural to the science rather than decorative.

### 1.3.4 Rationale and added value of the non-academic placement (and secondments)

No secondments are planned; the optional secondment provision (SR-07) is not used. The inter-sectoral component of FIELDWISE is instead a six-month non-academic placement at AGROVIR Kft. in Budaörs, Hungary (M25–M30), added at the end of the action as an extension of the European Fellowship under constraint CC-07 — the permitted up-to-six-month non-academic placement (SR-06), included here as an integral, justified and evaluated part of the proposal. AgroVIR co-leads the *Operational Transfer, Decision Value and Web MVP* work package from M16 and hosts the fellow on placement from M25 to M30.

**Added value for the project.** The placement makes the operational-transfer half of the proposal structural rather than asserted. The project's own decision-value framework claims (H5) that research-to-farm transfer is precisely where models break; a six-month period embedded in the company that runs the commercial farms is the strongest available evidence that the proposal takes its own gap seriously. It also answers directly the criticism recorded against the previous evaluation that the economic and technological route to users was insufficiently substantiated.

**Added value for the researcher's career.** The placement supplies the inter-sectoral half of the intended career progression — Plant Physiologist/Agronomist → EO/Geospatial Crop Scientist → independent researcher in transferable agricultural intelligence — through operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation and direct exposure to commercial agricultural-software requirements, none of which the academic host can provide. It is the segment of the profile that makes the fellow employable in precision-agriculture, irrigation-technology and FMIS companies as well as in academia, broadening employability within and beyond academia (EO-01).

**Why it must be inside the company and why it needs six months.** The placement work content is defined as four items that each depend on the company's own operational environment and customer-facing requirements: operational hardening of the prediction pipeline in a production FMIS environment; the nine-dimension operational assessment producing the AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation (D5.4); the FMIS integration roadmap written from inside the implementing company (D5.5); and requirements engineering and user testing with commercial growers. These deepen existing work-package content rather than adding a new strand, and they cannot be performed from the academic host, whose capacity is research infrastructure. The fellow is supervised on site during the placement by a named on-site supervisor at AgroVIR (Miklós Maróti), and the placement is deliberately positioned to serve the fellow's training rather than the host company's engineering. Consistent with the Guide for Applicants, the placement is described here in Part B-1 so that evaluators can assess its relevance and quality under this criterion.

claim_statuses.claim_summary: The action is a European Fellowship with a 6-month non-academic placement extension under CC-07 (no secondments), requiring two-way researcher–host knowledge transfer.
Host beneficiary is Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, Budapest, Hungary.
Confirmed 30-month duration: 24 months at ELTE (M1–M24) plus a 6-month placement at AgroVIR (M25–M30).

Lead supervisor is Prof. András Jung, Professor at the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics; remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging and field spectroscopy, geoinformatics; chairs the Steering Group.
Co-supervisor is Dr. Roland Hollós, ELTE Department of Meteorology; ML/meta-modelling and agro-meteorology; methodological lead and QA for model development and testing in WP3 and WP4.
The co-supervisor's primary employment being ELTE (rather than HUN-REN), as MSCA requires supervision at the beneficiary, is an open check.
Supervision is a two-person team at the beneficiary with non-overlapping responsibilities, interdisciplinary within the host (geoinformatics + meteorology/ML).
Supervisor and host previously prepared/submitted an MSCA-PF application, PLANTDIGISENSE (proposal 101284764, host ELTE), with the same fellow, evidencing supervisory experience at advanced level.
Whether ELTE has previously hosted a funded MSCA fellow (as distinct from submitting an application) is not evidenced.
Prof. Gábor Milics (MATE) is a named scientific advisor to the fellow, adding a second agronomy-facing supervision strand outside the governance structure.
Career Development Plan delivered as D1.3 Career Development Plan, agreed by M3, signed jointly by both supervisors and the fellow, reviewed at M6, M12, M16, M20 and M27.
Training comprises scientific competences (closing a named gap), management (PM, grant writing, IP/exploitation), seven transferable-skill strands, and teaching/public engagement.
Transferable-skills training including generative-AI literacy, open science/FAIR and research integrity satisfies the call's mandatory training requirement.
Teaching feedback via a co-designed ELTE MSc module unit, MSc thesis supervision and PhD field-experiment co-supervision; framed as an existing five-year teaching strength transferred.
Primary supervision of an ELTE MSc thesis may require formal ELTE affiliation/status the fellow will not automatically hold; falls back to co-supervision if unavailable.
Cadence: weekly supervisor one-to-one; weekly co-supervisor technical session through WP3/WP4 (M6–M21) tapering to monthly; monthly written progress record; quarterly CDP review.
Two-way researcher–host transfer: eleven ELTE→fellow competences and nine fellow→ELTE competences, genuinely bidirectional (geospatial/data science ↔ crop physiology/agronomy).
Wider academic–research–industry chain: MATE (source-domain data/validation), MVCRI (Hungary→Bulgaria transfer), AgroVIR (research→farm bridge).
Supervision, training and transfer map to call expected outcomes EO-01, EO-02, EO-03, EO-05, EO-07 and EO-08.
No secondments are planned; the optional secondment provision is not used, the inter-sectoral component being the non-academic placement.
Six-month non-academic placement at AGROVIR Kft. (M25–M30) under CC-07; AgroVIR co-leads WP5 from M16 and hosts the fellow M25–M30.

Placement added value: structural evidence for the operational-transfer gap (H5), answering prior-evaluation route-to-users criticism, and supplying the inter-sectoral career segment for employability.
